entities.name: Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena is the world's oldest surviving bank, founded in 1472 in Siena, Italy by the governing council of the Republic of Siena to provide low-interest loans to the city's poorest citizens. The bank has operated continuously for over 550 years through the fall of the Sienese Republic, Medici Florence's conquest, the Napoleonic Wars, Italian Unification, two World Wars, and multiple financial crises — an institutional continuity unmatched in banking history.

The Monte dei Paschi (Mount of the Pastures) was named for the grazing lands of the Sienese Maremma that backed the bank's initial capitalization. The bank's original mission was explicitly social: to provide credit to 'the poor and miserable citizens' of Siena who were exploited by private moneylenders. The bank's building in Siena's Piazza Salimbeni has served as its headquarters continuously since 1471, making it the world's longest-continuously-operating corporate address.

Monte dei Paschi nearly collapsed multiple times in the 21st century: in 2008-2012 from complex derivative contracts with Deutsche Bank and Nomura that concealed losses, and in 2016-2017 when it failed European bank stress tests. Italian and EU taxpayers have provided €15 billion in bailouts. The Italian state now owns 64% of the bank. Despite its crises, Monte dei Paschi's 550-year survival is itself remarkable — a testimony to the difficulty of allowing iconic institutions to fail and the political protection afforded to Italy's most historically significant financial institution.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena's 550-year continuous operation as the world's oldest surviving bank — from a 1472 social welfare institution for Siena's poor to a modern bank requiring €15 billion in bailouts — is an unparalleled study in institutional survival and the political impossibility of allowing iconic institutions to fail.
